paragraphs: Neural responses vary both because the image being viewed changes and because brain activity fluctuates even for a given image. This paper builds a joint model of these two sources of variability. Its goal is to predict the distribution of activity across a population of neurons, including fluctuations that neurons share.

The approach combines a deep network for stimulus-driven activity with a generative model based on normalizing flows for variability conditional on the stimulus. The flow component gives the model flexibility to represent correlated responses. The combined system can be trained end to end while avoiding sophisticated probabilistic approximations required by many latent-state approaches.

Trained on thousands of neurons from multiple mouse visual areas, the model improves predictions for previously unseen images over earlier leading models. It also recovers latent factors associated with pupil dilation and factors that vary with brain area or retinotopic location. These findings make it useful for examining how stimulus information, behavior, and population fluctuations jointly shape neural activity.
neurips-2021-a-flow-based-latent-state-g.tldr: A joint neural-network and normalizing-flow model predicts image-driven neural activity and shared fluctuations while recovering behavior-related latent factors.

paragraphs: This paper studies changes that unfold gradually in a sequence of observations collected over time. It addresses two related questions: whether the distribution generating the observations has changed, and where in the sequence that change occurs. A gradual transition makes these questions different from detecting a sudden jump between two distributions.

Much existing work concentrates on abrupt changes, which can be an unrealistic description of some applications. The proposed method instead accommodates gradual change without requiring a specific model of how the data were generated. It also avoids prescribing a particular data type or requiring advance knowledge of which distributional features will change.

The contribution combines this broad formulation with theoretical guarantees for both detection and localization. That combination matters because flexibility alone would not establish that a method can reliably identify or locate a change. The paper provides a statistically justified approach to gradual transitions while relaxing several modeling commitments that could otherwise restrict where a change-detection method applies.
neurips-2021-a-nonparametric-method-for-.tldr: A nonparametric method detects and locates gradual distribution changes with theoretical guarantees and without specifying which features change.

paragraphs: The paper examines adversarial robustness in k-nearest-neighbor classification: how little an input must change before the classifier assigns a different label. Finding a perturbation with minimum norm gives a way to evaluate this vulnerability. The work brings attention to a practical classifier outside the neural networks that dominate much adversarial-example research.

Its central idea is a geometric search using higher-order Voronoi cells, which organize the space according to nearest-neighbor relationships. Starting at the original input, the search expands outward into nearby cells until it reaches one with a different classification. This connects the search for an adversarial example to the classifier’s spatial decision structure.

To handle larger values of k, the authors introduce approximation steps. Across several datasets, these steps find label-changing perturbations with smaller norms than the compared baselines. The paper also analyzes dataset structure associated with its advantage. The empirical result supports the usefulness of the geometric approach without claiming that the scalable approximations always recover the minimum possible perturbation.
neurips-2021-adversarial-examples-for-k-.tldr: An outward geometric search finds adversarial examples for k-nearest-neighbor classifiers, with scalable approximations producing smaller perturbations than tested baselines.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether self-supervised learning can strengthen adversarially trained systems that recognize 3D point clouds. Robustness matters for applications such as autonomous driving, where altered input points can affect recognition. The study examines how auxiliary learning tasks interact with the architecture and the type of adversarial threat.

The experiments cover PointNet, DGCNN, and PCT, representing multilayer-perceptron, convolutional, and transformer approaches. Rather than treating self-supervision as uniformly beneficial, the authors study different proxy tasks and their applications. They find that appropriate choices substantially improve robustness compared with standard adversarial training in the evaluated settings.

Their analysis points to learning local features as a useful ingredient. Local processing can limit how perturbations at individual input points propagate toward the final prediction. This explanation also helps account for the stronger robustness obtained with DGCNN and the jigsaw proxy task. The findings therefore offer both an empirical improvement and an explanation for why particular combinations of architecture and self-supervision work well.
neurips-2021-adversarially-robust-3d-poi.tldr: Appropriately chosen self-supervised tasks improve adversarially trained point-cloud recognition, with local feature learning helping limit perturbation propagation.

paragraphs: Bandit learning becomes difficult when reward noise occasionally takes extremely large values. This paper considers noise whose tail probability is bounded by a power law with any positive exponent. Such a setting can allow moments of the noise to be undefined, placing it beyond assumptions used in many treatments of heavy-tailed observations.

The authors introduce a robust estimator called mean of medians. It first computes a sequence of empirical medians and then averages those medians. They use this estimator as a filter on reward signals, creating a general framework that can be attached to nearly any bandit-learning algorithm, including methods for multi-armed and linear bandits.

The framework obtains regret bounds similar to those associated with sub-Gaussian rewards, and the authors show near-optimal bounds even under very heavy-tailed noise. Experiments also support the method’s effectiveness. The central contribution is a reusable way to handle extreme reward corruption while retaining strong learning guarantees under the stated tail condition.
neurips-2021-breaking-the-moments-condit.tldr: A mean-of-medians reward filter enables broadly applicable bandit algorithms with near-optimal regret under super heavy-tailed noise.

paragraphs: Panoptic segmentation combines identifying semantic categories with separating individual object instances. This paper proposes COPS, an architecture that connects a convolutional neural network to a combinatorial optimization solver. The aim is to make the network’s predictions and the optimization procedure work together in producing the final image labeling.

The solver handles an asymmetric multiway cut problem that incorporates both semantic predictions and predicted boundaries. Crucially, the architecture allows training gradients to pass through that optimization problem. This makes it possible to directly optimize a smooth surrogate of panoptic quality, connecting learning to a measure of the combined segmentation result.

Experiments on Cityscapes and COCO show improvements from backpropagating through the solver relative to comparable approaches. The significance is that the optimization component participates in learning, rather than merely receiving predictions after training. The results demonstrate the usefulness of combining deep prediction with structured optimization on a demanding segmentation task and provide evidence for training the two as a single differentiable architecture.
neurips-2021-combinatorial-optimization-.tldr: COPS improves panoptic segmentation by training a neural network through a combinatorial solver using a smooth panoptic-quality objective.

paragraphs: Large clinical databases make finding relevant records increasingly difficult, especially when many instances lack labels. CROCS addresses this problem for cardiac signals by organizing them around patient attributes such as disease class, sex, and age. The intended capabilities are clustering signals and retrieving relevant examples using multiple attributes together.

The method uses supervised contrastive learning to bring signal representations toward learned embeddings called clinical prototypes. Each prototype is associated with a set of patient attributes. These learned reference points then support organizing and searching unlabeled cardiac signals, linking the representation space to clinically meaningful descriptions.

The authors report better clustering than DTC and demonstrate retrieval of relevant signals from a large database. They also find that the prototypes arrange themselves in ways that reflect patient attributes, supporting interpretation of the learned space. The contribution is therefore both a search-and-organization framework and a representation whose structure can be understood through the attributes used to train it.
neurips-2021-crocs-clustering-and-retrie.tldr: CROCS learns patient-attribute prototypes that support interpretable clustering and retrieval of unlabeled cardiac signals.

paragraphs: A Wasserstein barycenter expresses a geometric notion of a center among probability distributions. Computing it can be costly because many approximation algorithms depend exponentially on the dimension of the underlying space. This paper studies whether the problem can be compressed before solving it while preserving the quality of the resulting solution.

When the barycenter is restricted to n support points, the authors show that randomized reduction can bring the dimension down to O(log n), independently of the original dimension and the number of input distributions. Their guarantee preserves the cost of any reduced-space solution up to arbitrarily small error in the original space. Matching bounds establish optimality of the reduced dimension up to constant factors.

A second contribution constructs coresets that reduce the number of distributions involved. These can be combined with random projections, addressing both the dimensionality and the amount of input. Experiments support the computational benefit: dimensionality reduction speeds up computation while maintaining solution quality in the evaluated cases.
neurips-2021-dimensionality-reduction-fo.tldr: Random projections and coresets accelerate Wasserstein barycenter computation, with cost-preservation guarantees for barycenters restricted to n support points.

paragraphs: Few-shot language learning studies adaptation with limited examples, but separate research communities often evaluate methods differently. This paper argues that fragmented evaluations and weak experimental design make it difficult to tell which techniques work best or whether they improve on simple baselines. FLEX addresses the problem at the level of evaluation practice.

The authors introduce principles for rigorous, realistic, unified, and cost-sensitive assessment. One component, Sample Size Design, chooses benchmark designs to improve statistical accuracy and precision while keeping evaluation costs manageable. The resulting FLEX benchmark spans four few-shot transfer settings, includes zero-shot evaluation, and provides a public leaderboard across diverse language tasks.

The paper also introduces UniFew, a prompt-based model that aligns the prompt formats used during pretraining and finetuning. Despite its simplicity, it performs competitively with popular meta-learning and prompt-based methods. Together, the benchmark and model provide a common evaluation framework and a straightforward competitive approach, making comparison across few-shot research directions more meaningful.
neurips-2021-flex-unifying-evaluation-fo.tldr: FLEX supplies statistically careful few-shot NLP evaluation, alongside a simple prompt-based model competitive with more elaborate approaches.

paragraphs: Policy networks help continuous-control agents estimate and sample valuable actions. This paper examines them through the variational-inference view of reinforcement learning. With entropy or KL regularization, such networks perform amortized optimization: learning shared network parameters takes the place of directly optimizing the policy distribution for each situation.

The authors argue that a direct amortized mapping can produce suboptimal policy estimates and restrict the distributions the agent can represent. These restrictions can affect both performance and exploration. They therefore consider iterative amortized optimizers, a more flexible class that makes iteration part of the learned optimization process instead of relying only on a direct mapping.

The resulting method, iterative amortized policy optimization, improves performance over direct amortization on benchmark continuous-control tasks. The contribution connects a practical policy-design choice to an optimization perspective: how a policy is computed can constrain what the agent learns. The reported results support iterative amortization as a useful alternative in the evaluated tasks, rather than establishing that every direct policy mapping will be inadequate.
neurips-2021-iterative-amortized-policy-.tldr: Iterative amortized policy optimization uses a more flexible learned optimization process to improve continuous-control performance over direct policy mappings.

paragraphs: Attention mechanisms need positional information to handle inputs where location or order matters. This paper proposes learning that information through Fourier features rather than assigning each position a fixed token or vector. The method is designed to accommodate positions with multiple coordinates, such as locations within an image.

Each position passes through a learnable Fourier feature mapping, with a multilayer perceptron further modulating the encoding. This makes the positional representation trainable along with the model. The authors identify multidimensional spatial settings as particularly suitable, because the representation needs to capture Euclidean distances or more complicated relationships among positions.

Across several public benchmark tasks, the proposed encoding improves accuracy and allows faster convergence compared with existing methods. These results suggest that learning the positional mapping can benefit both the quality of the final model and its training progress. The contribution focuses on how spatial coordinates are represented for attention-based architectures, giving the model a way to adapt positional information to the task.
neurips-2021-learnable-fourier-features-.tldr: Trainable Fourier-based positional encodings improve accuracy and convergence on tested tasks involving multidimensional spatial information.

paragraphs: This paper creates a shared representation space for speech and text across languages. A speech encoder produces a fixed-size representation and is trained to align with the existing multilingual LASER text space using cosine loss. Related sentences can consequently be close even when their language or input modality differs.

The authors use similarity in this space to match Librivox audio in German, French, Spanish, and English against billions of Common Crawl sentences. This produces more than twenty thousand hours of aligned speech translations. Adding the mined data to speech-translation training significantly improves BLEU on CoVoST2 and MUST-C relative to a competitive baseline.

The same approach also matches speech directly to speech without first transcribing or translating it. This yields more than thirteen hundred hours of aligned multilingual audio. The findings show that shared embeddings can support large-scale collection of translation training pairs, including direct speech pairs for a research area constrained by scarce natural end-to-end data. The authors also state plans to release the mined corpora freely.
neurips-2021-multimodal-and-multilingual.tldr: A shared multilingual speech-and-text embedding space mines large translation corpora that improve evaluated speech-translation systems.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must evaluate or improve policies using already collected episodes. This paper studies how the amount of data needed depends on episode length. It considers time-homogeneous episodic environments with either tabular structure or a linear representation with anchor points, and assumes total reward is bounded above by one.

For policy evaluation, the authors obtain an error bound scaling roughly as the inverse square root of the number of episodes times minimum state-action visiting probability. It matches a lower bound up to logarithmic factors, without extra polynomial dependence on horizon or model size in higher-order terms. Policy optimization receives a related bound with an additional higher-order term involving the smaller of the state count and feature dimension.

The main result is that strong offline guarantees can be nearly independent of horizon under these assumptions. Coverage still matters through the minimum visiting probability. A recursion that controls total variance is central to the analysis, explaining how the authors avoid horizon factors present in earlier bounds.
neurips-2021-nearly-horizon-free-offline.tldr: Under bounded total reward and specified MDP structure, offline policy evaluation and optimization admit nearly horizon-free error guarantees.

paragraphs: Estimating causal effects often requires choosing variables to adjust for, and valid choices can differ in statistical precision. This paper studies optimal adjustment when causal graphs contain hidden and conditioned variables. In this setting, an optimal set need not exist, so identifying when one exists is itself a central problem.

The authors characterize optimality through an information-based quantity and derive a graphical condition that is both necessary and sufficient for existence. They also give a construction algorithm. The constructed set is valid whenever a valid adjustment set exists, and its adjustment information is at least as high as that of the compared Adjust-set.

The information result implies minimum asymptotic variance for estimators satisfying a specified information-theoretic relation. Experiments suggest benefits at relatively small sample sizes and often beyond that estimator class. More than 90% of randomly generated setups meet the optimality conditions; this supports the possibility of broad applicability without establishing the same rate for real-world causal graphs.
neurips-2021-necessary-and-sufficient-gr.tldr: A necessary-and-sufficient graphical criterion identifies when optimal causal adjustment exists, with variance guarantees for a specified estimator class.

paragraphs: Standard graph neural networks repeatedly aggregate neighboring features, producing node representations associated with rooted subtrees. Those representations can miss distinctions in graphs whose structure is not tree-like. Nested Graph Neural Networks address this expressive limitation by making local subgraphs the building blocks of a whole-graph representation.

For each node, NGNN extracts a surrounding subgraph and applies a base graph neural network to that subgraph. It then pools the resulting subgraph representations to describe the complete graph. The framework can wrap different base networks, allowing an existing architecture to represent richer local structure through the nested construction.

The authors prove that NGNN is strictly more expressive than the 1-WL procedure underlying standard message-passing expressiveness. In particular, it distinguishes almost all regular graphs of the studied kind where 1-WL fails. They report only a constant-factor increase in time complexity over standard GNNs. Across tested base networks and benchmark datasets, NGNN consistently improves performance and remains highly competitive, connecting the theoretical increase in expressiveness to empirical gains.
neurips-2021-nested-graph-neural-network.tldr: NGNN pools learned local-subgraph representations to exceed 1-WL expressiveness and improve tested graph classifiers with constant-factor additional time complexity.

paragraphs: Implicit planning combines learned world representations with end-to-end reinforcement learning. This paper examines planners inspired by value iteration, which has strong guarantees in fully specified tabular environments. Existing approaches either depend on that restrictive representation or construct local state neighborhoods over which to run the planning computation.

The authors identify a bottleneck when planning relies on scalar predictions for every state: inaccurate scalar estimates can hurt data efficiency. Their XLVIN method instead carries out planning in a high-dimensional latent space. Neural graph-algorithmic reasoning and contrastive self-supervision help keep these learned computations aligned with value iteration while avoiding that scalar bottleneck.

Across seven low-data settings spanning control, navigation, and Atari, XLVIN significantly improves data efficiency over value-iteration-based implicit planners and relevant model-free baselines. The authors also empirically verify close alignment with value iteration. The findings support transferring the structure of a planning algorithm into learned representations, while the reported alignment remains an empirical result rather than a claim of exact planning in every environment.
neurips-2021-neural-algorithmic-reasoner.tldr: XLVIN performs value-iteration-inspired planning in latent space, improving data efficiency in seven evaluated low-data reinforcement-learning settings.

paragraphs: Randomness in neural responses can reduce a network’s vulnerability to adversarial inputs. This paper investigates why, using geometric tools from computational neuroscience to examine internal representations. It compares standard networks, adversarially trained networks, and biologically inspired stochastic networks to understand how their responses to perturbations differ.

The analysis finds distinct geometric patterns across the three network types, indicating different mechanisms for robust representations. In stochastic networks, representations of clean and adversarially altered stimuli overlap. The authors also extend the investigation beyond vision and show that neural stochasticity improves adversarial robustness in the evaluated auditory models.

The results do not portray stochasticity as an unqualified benefit. Competing geometric effects mediate a tradeoff between performance on clean inputs and performance under adversarial perturbations. By quantifying that relationship, the work helps explain both the usefulness and the costs of response randomness. It also provides a way to compare robust perception strategies in trained and stochastic networks, informing how stochasticity may benefit machine and biological computation.
neurips-2021-neural-population-geometry-.tldr: Geometric analysis explains how neural stochasticity can improve visual and auditory adversarial robustness while creating a tradeoff with clean-input performance.

paragraphs: When several agents cooperate over a sequence of decisions, assigning responsibility for an outcome is more complicated than identifying one isolated action. This paper formalizes blame attribution in cooperative multi-agent Markov decision processes. It examines methods drawn from cooperative game theory and defines properties that a desirable attribution rule should satisfy.

The analysis shows that familiar methods can conflict with those properties. Shapley-value attribution does not provide the studied performance incentive, while the Banzhaf index can assign excessive blame. These findings show why importing a recognized attribution method does not automatically produce the desired combination of fairness and incentives in sequential decision making.

The authors introduce a method with a distinctive combination of satisfied properties. It gains those properties by allowing under-blaming, which sacrifices some explanatory power. They also extend attribution to account for uncertainty about agents’ policies. Experiments validate qualitative properties and investigate robustness to that uncertainty, making the tradeoffs between explanation, fairness, and behavioral incentives explicit.
neurips-2021-on-blame-attribution-for-ac.tldr: A formal study of multi-agent blame identifies incentive and fairness failures in familiar methods and proposes an alternative that deliberately permits under-blaming.

paragraphs: In some sequential decisions, learning the current state of the environment has a cost. This paper studies agents that can pay to observe the state fully before acting or act without an immediate observation using information from the past. The setting captures a tradeoff between acquiring information and conserving the resources needed to obtain it.

The authors formalize this structure through action-contingent noiselessly observable MDPs, a special class of partially observable problems. For tabular environments, they develop a probably approximately correct learning algorithm. Its guarantee gives substantially tighter bounds than generic partially observable learning algorithms on how many episodes perform worse than a near-optimal standard.

For continuous states, the paper proposes a new way to incorporate observation information into modern reinforcement-learning methods. In several simulated environments, this leads to significantly faster learning than compared partially observable approaches. The contributions show that exploiting the option of costly but complete observation can improve both theoretical learning guarantees and practical learning speed in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2021-reinforcement-learning-with.tldr: Algorithms that exploit optional costly state observations improve learning guarantees and simulated learning speed for a structured class of partially observable problems.

paragraphs: Hyperbolic space is useful for embedding hierarchical data, but its numerical representation can undermine learning. Ordinary floating-point arithmetic introduces errors that affect performance. The paper argues that simply increasing precision does not resolve the problem and can be expensive on GPUs that lack native support for precision beyond double.

The proposed solution represents hyperbolic space using multi-component floating-point values in the Poincaré upper-half-space model. This changes how the geometry is represented numerically while remaining feasible on GPUs. The authors present it as a simple approach to accurate learning in hyperbolic space, addressing the numerical representation directly.

Theoretical analysis and experiments show small numerical error for the proposed model. On embedding tasks across multiple datasets, representations using multi-component floats gain capacity and run significantly faster on GPUs than prior work. The findings connect numerical accuracy to practical modeling ability: a useful geometry must also be represented in a way that computation can handle reliably and efficiently.
neurips-2021-representing-hyperbolic-spa.tldr: Multi-component floats enable accurate hyperbolic representations that improve embedding capacity and GPU speed in the evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: A classifier’s accuracy and the reliability of its confidence estimates are different properties. Calibration concerns whether predictive uncertainty is estimated appropriately. Earlier reports suggested that newer, more accurate neural networks often had worse calibration. This paper revisits that relationship for recent leading image-classification models.

The authors systematically compare accuracy and calibration and find that some of the most recent models are also among the best calibrated. Models without convolutions stand out in this respect. Previously reported tendencies, including worsening calibration with distribution shift or increasing model size, are less pronounced in the newer architectures they examine.

The differences are not fully explained by model size or the amount of pretraining. This suggests that architecture is a major contributor to calibration behavior, although the result does not establish architecture as its sole cause. The study changes how the earlier pattern should be interpreted: increasing accuracy does not imply deteriorating uncertainty estimates across the model generations evaluated here.
neurips-2021-revisiting-the-calibration-.tldr: Recent image classifiers can be both accurate and well calibrated, with architectural differences appearing to matter beyond size and pretraining.

paragraphs: SSL-HSIC learns image representations by directly measuring statistical dependence. It encourages representations of transformed images to retain information about image identity while controlling their kernelized variance. This provides a self-supervised objective grounded in dependence rather than an indirect estimate of mutual information.

The framework also explains aspects of existing methods. The authors show that InfoNCE approximately implements SSL-HSIC with a somewhat different regularizer, helping explain why that bound can behave better than mutual information itself. They also connect SSL-HSIC to BYOL through the local neighborhoods of samples that the methods learn.

The proposed objective can be optimized in time linear in batch size without restrictive data assumptions or indirect mutual-information estimators. With or without a target network, it matches leading results on the evaluated ImageNet linear classification, semi-supervised, and transfer tasks, including segmentation and depth estimation. The contribution therefore combines a competitive learning method with a statistical perspective that links several approaches to self-supervised representation learning.
neurips-2021-self-supervised-learning-wi.tldr: SSL-HSIC directly optimizes statistical dependence, connects InfoNCE and BYOL conceptually, and matches leading results on evaluated representation-learning tasks.

paragraphs: The null space of a higher-order Laplacian encodes nontrivial topological structure in a manifold or network. This paper investigates the geometry of the resulting homology embedding. Its motivation parallels spectral clustering, where understanding a graph Laplacian’s null-space representation has enabled useful algorithms and theoretical analysis.

The authors study a connected sum of manifolds by treating its homology embedding as a perturbation of the direct sum of the component embeddings. This viewpoint leads to an algorithm that decomposes the embedding into subspaces associated with simpler topological components. The aim is to make the embedding’s internal structure reveal how the underlying topology is assembled.

They apply the framework to detecting shortest homologous loops, a problem that is NP-hard in general. The resulting spectral loop-detection algorithm scales better than existing methods and works effectively on varied data, including point clouds and images. These results demonstrate an algorithmic use for the decomposition without implying that the general computational difficulty of shortest-loop detection has disappeared.
neurips-2021-the-decomposition-of-the-hi.tldr: Decomposing higher-order homology embeddings exposes simpler topological components and supports scalable spectral loop detection.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning performance can depend strongly on hyperparameter choices. Population-based AutoRL tries to automate these choices by adjusting hyperparameters during training, producing schedules rather than relying on one fixed configuration. This paper addresses the need to tune both numerical settings and categorical choices within that process.

The starting point is PB2, which models online hyperparameter optimization as a time-varying Gaussian-process bandit problem but supports only continuous variables. The authors introduce a hierarchical approach for mixed continuous and categorical inputs. A new time-varying bandit algorithm is designed specifically for population-based training, and the approach comes with a provable efficiency result.

Evaluation on Procgen shows that explicitly modeling the dependence between data augmentation and other hyperparameters improves generalization. This matters because selecting an augmentation and tuning other settings are not necessarily separable decisions. The paper extends the range of choices that population-based optimization can handle while providing empirical evidence that accounting for their interactions benefits reinforcement learning in the tested benchmark.
neurips-2021-tuning-mixed-input-hyperpar.tldr: A provably efficient hierarchical bandit approach jointly tunes continuous and categorical hyperparameters during population-based reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Images contain both global factors, such as lighting, and local factors, such as an object’s color or size. This paper introduces COMET to discover both kinds of concepts within one unsupervised framework. The motivation is to avoid restricting concept discovery to either whole-scene variation or individual objects.

COMET represents concepts as separate energy functions and learns them by recomposing the input image. The authors find that this process captures independent factors without additional supervision. Image generation is then formulated as optimization over the learned energy functions, allowing discovered concepts to be rearranged and combined when producing samples.

The learned concepts also generalize across the settings studied. The authors demonstrate composition between separate image modalities and with concepts learned by another COMET instance trained on a different dataset. These findings support energy functions as a common representation for diverse visual factors. The contribution combines concept discovery with a generation procedure that makes the discovered pieces usable in new compositions, including combinations across independently trained models.
neurips-2021-unsupervised-learning-of-co.tldr: COMET discovers global and local visual concepts as energy functions that can be recombined to generate images across studied modalities and datasets.
